```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 7)
```

Models become useful when their parameters are estimated from data. Here we
generate "observed" data from an SIR epidemic with known parameters, then
recover the transmission rate $\beta$ by **least squares**: choose the
$\beta$ that makes the model curve closest to the observations.

# Simulate noisy observations

```{r}
library(deSolve)

sir <- function(time, state, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(state, parms)), {
    dS <- -beta * S * I / N
    dI <-  beta * S * I / N - gamma * I
    dR <-  gamma * I
    list(c(dS, dI, dR))
  })
}

N <- 1000
gamma <- 0.2                  # assume the infectious period is known (5 days)
days <- 0:60

model_I <- function(beta) {
  out <- ode(c(S = N - 1, I = 1, R = 0), days, sir,
             c(beta = beta, gamma = gamma, N = N))
  out[, "I"]
}

set.seed(10)
true_beta <- 0.5
observed <- rpois(length(days), model_I(true_beta))   # Poisson observation noise
```

# Define and minimise the error

```{r}
sse <- function(beta) sum((observed - model_I(beta))^2)

fit <- optimize(sse, interval = c(0.1, 1))
beta_hat <- fit$minimum
beta_hat                          # close to the true value 0.5
beta_hat / gamma                  # estimated R0 (true value 2.5)
```

# Compare the fitted curve with the data

```{r}
plot(days, observed, pch = 16, xlab = "Day", ylab = "Infectious people")
lines(days, model_I(beta_hat), col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("Observed", "Fitted SIR"), pch = c(16, NA),
       lty = c(NA, 1), col = c("black", "red"))
```

# See why it works: the error curve

```{r}
beta_grid <- seq(0.3, 0.7, by = 0.01)
plot(beta_grid, sapply(beta_grid, sse), type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "beta", ylab = "Sum of squared errors")
abline(v = beta_hat, lty = 2, col = "red")
```

The error has a clear minimum near the true $\beta$. In a real analysis you
would also estimate $\gamma$, report uncertainty, and use a likelihood
appropriate for count data, but the logic is exactly this.
